183.title: Sheep without a shepherd (Mark 6:30–44)
183.hook: he looks at the crowd with compassion and feeds five thousand
183.howItsDone: Many Christians connect the feeding of the five thousand with communion, where bread is blessed, broken and given, and churches often run food banks and shared meals with this story in mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John's head: a ruler's oath, and a good man killed for it. Your line was careless words cost lives.

The twelve come back from their travels full of stories, and exhausted. So many people are coming and going that they don't even have time to eat. Jesus says, come away with me to a quiet place and rest a while. They get in the boat. The crowd sees, runs around the shore on foot, and gets there first. The boat lands, and there they are. Thousands. The day off is gone before it starts. Mark tells us what Jesus felt.
screen: `NO TIME EVEN TO EAT.` → `COME AWAY AND REST.` → `THE CROWD GETS THERE FIRST.`

segments.voice: In the old King James Bible, Jesus "saw much people, and was moved with compassion toward them, because they were as sheep not having a shepherd." Moved with compassion is a gut word in Greek, about the insides: compassion felt deep in the body. And sheep without a shepherd is an old phrase in Israel's scriptures for a people with no one to guide or protect them. So he teaches them many things, until the day is far spent. Then it's late, and the disciples do the sensible thing: send them away to buy food. Jesus answers: "Give ye them to eat." You give them something. They do the math out loud: should they go and buy two hundred pennyworth of bread? He asks, what have you got? Five loaves and two fish. He has everyone sit in groups on the grass. Mark notices it was green, which some read as a hint of spring. Then he takes the loaves, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks the bread, and gives it to the disciples to hand out. Take, bless, break, give: Christian readers hear those same four actions again at the Last Supper, and at the communion table today. Everyone eats and is satisfied, and the leftovers fill twelve baskets. Some readers smile that there's one for each disciple who said send them away. About five thousand men, Mark says; Matthew adds, besides women and children. Christians have read it as a miracle of Jesus's power and a picture of God feeding his people. Some also notice he didn't let the disciples off the hook. He started with their little and put it in their hands.

184.title: It is I (Mark 6:45–52)
184.hook: walking on the lake at night: take heart, it is I, do not be afraid
184.howItsDone: Christians often turn to this story in times of fear or long struggle, and some pray its words, be of good cheer, be not afraid, for people facing a long night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a crowd like sheep without a shepherd, met with compassion, and five loaves in the disciples' hands. Your line was you give them something.

Straight after the feeding, Jesus sends the disciples off in the boat ahead of him, sends the crowd home, and climbs a hill alone to pray. Night falls. Out on the lake, the wind turns against them. They row, and row, and get nowhere. Hours of it, arms burning, the shore not getting any closer. Some problems are like that: rowing since sundown, getting nowhere. Then, in the last watch of the night, someone sees a figure on the water. Walking.
screen: `ALONE ON THE HILL TO PRAY.` → `ROWING AGAINST THE WIND.` → `A FIGURE ON THE WATER.`

segments.voice: In the old King James Bible: "he saw them toiling in rowing; for the wind was contrary unto them: and about the fourth watch of the night he cometh unto them, walking upon the sea, and would have passed by them." He saw them. From the hill, in the dark, he's been watching them struggle. The fourth watch is the last stretch of the night, before dawn. Then a strange phrase: he would have passed by them. Readers take it in different ways. Some hear an echo of the old stories where God passes by Moses on the mountain and Elijah at the cave, showing himself as he goes. The disciples think it's a ghost, and they scream. He speaks at once: "Be of good cheer: it is I; be not afraid." Take heart. It is I. Don't be afraid. In Greek, it is I is two words, ego eimi, which can also mean simply, I am. Some Christians hear in it the name God gives Moses at the burning bush: I am. Then he climbs into the boat, and the wind stops. You might expect joy. Mark gives us something more honest: they were utterly astonished, "For they considered not the miracle of the loaves: for their heart was hardened." They'd just seen five thousand fed, and it hadn't sunk in. And Mark's version has no Peter stepping out onto the water; that's in Matthew. Here it's just Jesus, the dark, the wind, and three phrases for frightened people.
screen: `HE SAW THEM TOILING IN ROWING.` · `HE WOULD HAVE PASSED BY THEM.` · `IT IS I — EGO EIMI, I AM.` · `THEIR HEART WAS HARDENED.`

Imagine standing near them and saying, simply, take heart. If you pray, you can pray the words from the story for them: be of good cheer, be not afraid.
Ego eimi, Greek for it is I, or simply I am: what Jesus said to frightened men in a boat before dawn.

185.title: Wherever he went (Mark 6:53–56)
185.hook: villages lay the sick in the marketplaces just to touch his fringe
185.howItsDone: Many Christians bring the needs of others into prayer by name, alone or aloud in church, and many congregations keep prayer lists for the sick of their community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a figure on the water before dawn, and three phrases: take heart. It is I, ego eimi. Don't be afraid.

The boat lands at Gennesaret, a fertile plain on the lake's western shore. The moment Jesus steps out, someone recognizes him. Then it's like watching news spread before phones. People run through the whole region. Anyone with someone sick at home picks them up, mat and all, and carries them to wherever they've heard he is. Village, town, farm, it doesn't matter. Today is just four verses long: no big speech, no single story, a snapshot of what it was like.

Here's the last verse, in the old King James Bible: "And whithersoever he entered, into villages, or cities, or country, they laid the sick in the streets, and besought him that they might touch if it were but the border of his garment: and as many as touched him were made whole." The streets here are the marketplaces, the open squares at the heart of every town. Picture the busiest square you know, lined with people on mats, waiting. And what do they ask for? Not a speech, not even a word. Just to touch the border of his garment. Remember the woman in the crowd, a week ago? What she did in secret, a whole region now does in the open. The border, in Greek, is kraspedon, a fringe or tassel. The law of Moses told the people of Israel to wear tassels on the corners of their garments, with a thread of blue, to remember God's commandments. Many Jews still wear them today, called tzitzit. So the fringe they reached for was very likely one of those: Jesus dressed as an observant Jew, and the sick reaching for the reminder of God's commands on his clothes. With that, the second part of Mark closes. Seeds, storms and loaves. The sower from a boat. Why parables. A lamp on a stand. Seed growing secretly. Asleep on a cushion. Legion. Go home and tell. The hem of his garment. Talitha koum. The carpenter at home. Travel light. John's head. Sheep without a shepherd. It is I. And now, wherever he went. Next, Mark asks the question straight out: who is this?

Picture setting their mat down in the square. If you pray, you can bring their need to God by name, the way the villages brought theirs; if you don't, hold them in mind, and ask who could help them that you could reach.
Kraspedon, the fringe or tassel on his cloak that a whole region reached for, villages and towns carrying their sick to touch.
Your line: touch the fringe. Mats in every marketplace, hands reaching for one thread. Part two of Mark, done.

186.title: Washed hands (Mark 7:1–13)
186.hook: he challenges traditions used to dodge caring for parents
186.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold sacred Tradition alongside scripture, while many Protestant churches weigh every tradition against scripture; many Christians read this passage as a call to check their own customs against love of God and neighbor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sick were laid in the marketplaces, reaching for his fringe, the kraspedon. Your line was touch the fringe.

A new part of Mark, chapters seven to nine, with one question underneath it all: who is this? It opens at a meal. Some Pharisees and teachers of the law have come up from Jerusalem, and they notice that some of Jesus's disciples are eating without first washing their hands in the ritual way. It's not about germs. It's about holiness, the careful washing that set apart an ordinary meal as something done before God. They ask Jesus why his followers don't keep it. And his answer is about something much bigger than hands.
screen: `MARK SEVEN TO NINE BEGINS.` → `A MEAL, AND UNWASHED HANDS.` → `WHY DON'T THEY KEEP IT?`

segments.voice: Mark explains the custom for his readers: the Pharisees, he says, wash their hands carefully before eating, and wash cups and pots too, keeping the tradition of the elders. It was, and is, a beautiful practice. Observant Jews today still wash their hands with a blessing before eating bread. A fair question. Jesus answers with the prophet Isaiah, in the old King James Bible: "This people honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." Then his real charge: "laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men." And an example. The commandment says honor your father and mother, which included caring for them in old age. But, he says, you've allowed someone to declare what they own Corban, dedicated to God, and then use that to refuse their parents any help. A holy word, used as a loophole. Jewish teachers themselves later wrote rules to release vows that hurt parents, so they saw the danger too. Tradition, in Greek paradosis, means what's handed over, passed from hand to hand. Christians have traditions of their own, and they don't all weigh them the same way. Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold sacred Tradition alongside scripture as a way God's word is handed on. Many Protestants give scripture the final word over any tradition. Read that way, the passage is a warning to anyone with traditions, churches included: a habit meant to bring you closer to God can end up used to dodge the people God asked you to love.
screen: `THE TRADITION OF THE ELDERS.` · `LIPS NEAR, HEART FAR.` · `CORBAN: A HOLY LOOPHOLE.` · `PARADOSIS — WHAT'S HANDED ON.`

segments.voice: Think of something you do regularly because it's good: a prayer routine, if you pray, a family ritual, a rule you keep at work. Ask what it was for, and then, honestly, whether it's ever become a reason to avoid something, or someone. Don't judge yourself, just look; if you pray, you can ask God to keep the heart of it alive in you.
Tradition. From the Greek paradosis, what's handed on. A gift, unless it's used to dodge the love it was meant to carry.
Your line: keep the heart of it. Not just lips near: a heart near is the point. See you tomorrow.

187.title: What comes out (Mark 7:14–23)
187.hook: it's not what goes in that defiles, but what comes out of the heart
187.howItsDone: Christians do not, as a rule, keep the Torah's food laws, and some point to this passage when asked why; some also practice an examination of conscience at the end of the day, looking back over what they said and did.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was tradition, what's handed on, and a holy word used as a loophole. Your line was keep the heart of it.

A whole day of careful eating: vegetables, water, vitamins. Then someone cuts in on the highway, or a coworker takes credit for the work, and what comes out is something nobody's grandmother should hear. Everything that went in was careful. What came out wasn't. After the argument about washed hands, Jesus calls the whole crowd back to him and says, listen, all of you, and understand. Then he says something so short it sounds like a riddle.
screen: `CAREFUL ABOUT WHAT GOES IN.` → `THEN SOMEONE CUTS YOU OFF.` → `LISTEN, ALL OF YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the riddle, in the old King James Bible: "There is nothing from without a man, that entering into him can defile him: but the things which come out of him, those are they that defile the man." Defile, in Greek, means to make common, to make ordinary something that was meant to be set apart. Later, indoors, the disciples ask him about it, and he's a bit exasperated again: "Are ye so without understanding also?" Food goes into the stomach, he says, not into the heart, and then out again. But "from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts," and he names a long list: thefts, murders, greed, deceit, envy, pride, foolishness. That's what really makes a person unclean. Mark adds a short note of his own here; the King James words it purging all meats, and some Christian readers take it as Jesus declaring all foods clean. Some Christians point to it when asked why they don't keep the food laws of the Torah. Jews who keep kosher understand those laws as God's commandments to Israel, and keep them with devotion; and scholars differ on how much Mark's note meant at the time. Either way, the center of the teaching is the heart. In the Bible, the heart isn't only feelings. It's where you think, decide and choose: the kitchen where words get cooked before they're served. So Jesus moves the question from the plate to the source. Not only, what did I take in today? But, what came out?
screen: `NOTHING FROM WITHOUT CAN DEFILE.` · `DEFILE — TO MAKE COMMON.` · `OUT OF THE HEART PROCEED.` · `THE HEART: WHERE YOU CHOOSE.`

segments.voice: Replay the last day: not what you ate or watched, but what you said, the kind words, the sharp ones, the joke at someone's expense, the complaint you repeated. Without punishing yourself, notice where each one came from: tired, scared, jealous, generous, glad. If you pray, you can ask God for a clean heart; if not, just choose one word you'd like to say more of.
Defile, what Jesus said doesn't come from the plate but from the heart: evil thoughts, not food, are what truly defile a person.
Your line: from the heart. What comes out shows what's inside. Day one hundred eighty-seven, complete.

188.title: Crumbs under the table (Mark 7:24–30)
188.hook: a Syrophoenician mother talks back to Jesus and wins
188.carry: even the dogs eat the crumbs
188.howItsDone: Some Christians look to the Syrophoenician woman as a model of bold, persistent prayer for others, and some churches read her story when speaking about welcome for outsiders.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was defile: not what goes in, but what comes out of the heart. Your line was from the heart.

Jesus slips into a house and wants nobody to know he's there. He has gone north, over the border, to the borders of Tyre and Sidon, Gentile cities on the coast. It doesn't work: Mark says he could not be hid. A woman finds him. She isn't Jewish, and she has no claim on him at all. But her young daughter has an unclean spirit, Mark says, and the mother falls at his feet and begs. What follows is an uncomfortable conversation, and readers still argue over it.
screen: `A HOUSE, AND NO ONE TO KNOW.` → `NORTH, OVER THE BORDER.` → `A MOTHER AT HIS FEET.`

segments.voice: Mark tells us exactly who she is: "The woman was a Greek, a Syrophenician by nation." Greek-speaking, from the Phoenician coast of Syria. An outsider, in every way. And Jesus's answer, in the old King James Bible, is hard to hear: "Let the children first be filled: for it is not meet to take the children's bread, and to cast it unto the dogs." The children are Israel. The dogs are everyone else. Mark's Greek uses a small form of the word for dog, the kind kept in the house, but it still stings. She doesn't walk away, and she doesn't argue that she isn't one. She picks up his picture and turns it: "Yes, Lord: yet the dogs under the table eat of the children's crumbs." Fine. Then I'll take the crumbs. Anyone who's watched kids eat knows the dog under the table eats well. And Jesus says: "For this saying go thy way; the devil is gone out of thy daughter." She goes home and finds the child lying in bed, well. Christians read this conversation in several ways. Some say Jesus was testing her faith, and she passed. Some say he was voicing what people around him thought, so that her answer would overturn it. Others say plainly that she changed his mind, and that Mark lets us see it. Either way, her daughter is healed for this saying. And notice the word first. Children first, not children only. Right after this, Jesus heads into more Gentile country. The crumbs are about to become a feast.
screen: `A GREEK, A SYROPHOENICIAN.` · `THE CHILDREN'S BREAD, AND THE DOGS.` · `YET THE DOGS EAT THE CRUMBS.` · `CHILDREN FIRST, NOT ONLY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you love who needs something they can't ask for themselves: a child who needs help at school, a parent navigating doctors, a friend facing a system that keeps saying no. Picture yourself, like this mother, refusing to take the first no as the last word, respectful, clever, stubborn, and ask what you would say. If you pray, you can bring their need to God as boldly as she did.
Syrophenician, the outsider mother, Greek-speaking from the Phoenician coast, whose sharp reply about crumbs won healing for her daughter.

189.title: Be opened (Mark 7:31–37)
189.hook: he puts fingers in a deaf man's ears, sighs, and says ephphatha
189.howItsDone: In the Catholic rite of baptism, the priest may touch the ears and mouth of the newly baptized and say ephphatha, praying that they will hear and proclaim God's word; some Christians pray the word for open ears and hearts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Syrophenician mother who wouldn't take no, and won healing for her daughter. Your line was even the dogs eat the crumbs.

Jesus takes the long way back. In the King James text he leaves the coasts of Tyre and Sidon and comes to the Sea of Galilee through the ten cities, the Decapolis, where the man called Legion went home to tell his story. Maybe that's why people there bring someone to him: a man who is deaf and can hardly speak. They beg Jesus to lay his hand on him. What Jesus does next is so physical, so hands-on, that some readers find it almost awkward. Mark keeps every gesture, and one Aramaic word.
screen: `THE LONG WAY AROUND.` → `BACK IN THE TEN CITIES.` → `A MAN WHO CANNOT HEAR.`

segments.voice: First, Jesus takes the man aside, away from the crowd. No show, just the two of them. Then he speaks the man's language, the language of touch. He puts his fingers in the man's ears. He spits and touches his tongue. Then, in the old King James Bible, "looking up to heaven, he sighed, and saith unto him, Ephphatha, that is, Be opened." He sighed: a groan, a deep breath out. Mark doesn't explain it. Some hear compassion, some hear prayer, some hear grief at all the ways the world is closed. Ephphatha is Aramaic, like talitha koum, and Mark translates it: be opened. "And straightway his ears were opened, and the string of his tongue was loosed, and he spake plain." The crowd can't keep quiet about it: "He hath done all things well: he maketh both the deaf to hear, and the dumb to speak." Dumb is the old word for unable to speak. Readers who know the prophet Isaiah hear his promise that one day the ears of the deaf would be unstopped and the tongue of the mute would sing. And the word lives on in church. In the Catholic baptism rite, the priest may touch the ears and mouth of the newly baptized and say ephphatha, praying that they'll soon hear God's word and speak it. That closes a week. Sheep without a shepherd. It is I. Wherever he went. Tradition. What comes out. Crumbs under the table. And one word, sighed toward heaven: be opened.
screen: `TAKEN ASIDE, AWAY FROM THE CROWD.` · `FINGERS, SPIT AND A SIGH.` · `EPHPHATHA — BE OPENED.` · `HE HATH DONE ALL THINGS WELL.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let the obvious sounds come and pass, then go looking for the hidden ones: the hum of a machine, your own heartbeat, wind against a window, a bird far off. Pick one and give it your full attention, as if you'd never heard it before. If you pray, you can offer the word to God: ephphatha.
Ephphatha. Aramaic for be opened, sighed by Jesus with his fingers in a deaf man's ears.
Your line: a sound you usually ignore. Fingers, a sigh, and ears opened. Twenty-seven weeks, done.
